title: Telling it your way
job: Retell a known story in your own register
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: ataḥ + <the moral of it> + iti + aham + jānāmi

rules.text: THE TALE IS NAMED IN ENGLISH AND ITS ACTORS ARE COMMON NOUNS. A known story is known by its names, and a name on this course rides unindexed: written into a line it would be a word with no row behind it, untappable and untaught. So the collection and the tale are named in English in the notes, and the lion, the hare and the forest each get a row of their own. rāmaḥ and sītā remain the only two names this course writes.

siṃhaḥ is masculine and takes siṃham when something is done to it or said to it; śaśakaḥ is masculine and appears here only as the one acting; vanam is neuter, so the forest looked at and the forest gone to are the same shape, and vane is 'in the forest'. Every shape this module shows is listed on its own row, and no shape is guessed from a neighbour.

kathā is a story, feminine, and it is A ROW OF ITS OWN beside L1-M2's kathayatu. The two share a root and nothing else on this course: kathā is the thing told, kathayatu is the asking to tell, and neither is a shape of the other. kathām is the shape when the story is what somebody tells.

THE PAST OF A TALE IS THE PAST THE COURSE ALREADY HAS. L4-M8's āsīt opens it, because a state that simply stood in the past needs it; the participial past carries every event; L3-M1's absolutives pack two legs into one breath. THE IMPERFECT AS A SYSTEM STAYS REFUSED — agacchat, akarot and abhavat are not written here or anywhere, and neither is the conditional agamiṣyat. A fable is exactly where a grammar would reach for them, which is why the refusal is restated at the fable.

THE PARTICIPIAL PAST AGREES WITH ITS SUBJECT, AND IN A TALE THE SUBJECT IS THE ANIMAL. saḥ … uktavān, sā … uktavatī: the fork this course has always made at the speaker is made here at the character instead. And THE PLURAL PARTICIPIAL PAST IS WRITTEN NOWHERE, so a tale is told about one actor at a time and the animals act in the singular.

THE SAME EVENT TOLD TWICE IS THE MODULE'S WHOLE PAYLOAD, AND IT OPENS NO FORM AT ALL. Once in the neutral voice the learner owns — short sentences, the participial past, the four sequencers — and once with the classical register's move, L4-M7's agentless passive: ekaḥ siṃhaḥ vane āsīt against vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ āsīt iti ucyate. Nobody is named as telling it, and that is what makes the second one sound like a book.

English tells a fable in the simple past and marks the register with vocabulary — 'once upon a time', 'thereupon'. Here the register is carried by SYNTAX: the passive, the weight of the nouns, the length of the sentence. A retelling that swaps only the nouns has not changed register at all, and that is this module's mistake plate.

English shifts a quoted line when it reports it — 'he said there WAS a lion'. Nothing shifts here. The quote keeps its own tense and its own speaker, iti stands behind it, and vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ asti iti śaśakaḥ uktavān has a present tense inside a past-tense sentence and is entirely correct.

THE VOCATIVE IS REFUSED FOR THE FIFTH TIME, AND A FABLE'S DIALOGUE IS WHERE IT IS WANTED MOST. An animal in a tale addresses another animal, and every language with a vocative would use one. This one has four declensions' worth of them, no second person to hang them on, and a form one short vowel from the course's commonest word. The dialogue here is addressed with the accusative — siṃham uktavān — and with nothing else.

STILL WRITTEN NOWHERE, and named here because a tale is where each would be reached for. Every imperfect but āsīt; -syat and the conditional; the productive bare -ta participle, of which jātam and niṣiddhaḥ remain the only two frozen members; the plural participial past; svasā; every -si present; and any new proper noun at all.

words.note: L1-M8's 'one' in its feminine shape, because kathā is feminine. It is doing the work English gives to 'a'.
A story, feminine. It shares a root with L1-M2's kathayatu and is NOT a shape of it: one is the thing told, the other is the asking to tell.
L1-M3's 'there is'. It opens a tale the way English opens one with 'there was', and the tale itself then moves to āsīt.

sentences.trap: ekā and not ekam. The numeral copies the gender of the noun beside it, and kathā is feminine — the -ā at the end of both words is the whole of the agreement.
sentences.sound: ay-KAA ka-THAA AS-ti. Both long ā's are held, and the th of kathā is an aspirated t: a t with a puff of breath after it, never the th of English 'think'.

variations.cue: My mother told me a story.
variations.changed: the story becomes the thing told, which is the -ām shape, and a teller is named

variations.cue: I like the story.
variations.changed: the tale becomes the thing liked, in L1-M1's frame, with the person in the 'to me' shape

variations.cue: Do you like the story?
variations.changed: asked of the listener, which is how a retelling is usually offered

sentences.usage: The opening of a retelling. The tale below is the lion and the hare, from the Pañcatantra — named here in English, because a name written into a Sanskrit line on this course would be a word with no row behind it.
sentences.mnemonic: Say there is one, then tell it.

sentences.cue: There was once a lion in a forest.

words.note: L1-M8's 'one', masculine here. In a tale it is exactly English 'a certain' — the lion nobody has met yet.
A lion, masculine. siṃham is the shape when something is done to him or said to him. The ṃ is inside the word, as in saṃskṛtam, and is written in full.
The forest, neuter, cued for the word and not for the case: vanam names it and is the place gone TO, and vane is L1-M7's 'in' shape on it.
L4-M8's one imperfect, third singular. It says how something STOOD, which is all a tale's first sentence ever does.

sentences.trap: āsīt and not jātam. jātam is for what happened; āsīt is for what simply was, and a tale's opening state is always the second of the two.
sentences.sound: ay-KAH SIM-hah VA-nay AA-seet. The ṃ of siṃhaḥ closes the first syllable and the h after it is the full breathy consonant, not a silent letter.

variations.cue: There was once a hare in a forest.
variations.changed: the other actor opens the tale instead, which is how the same story is told from the other side

variations.cue: There was once a lion in a city.
variations.changed: the place moves to one the course has owned since Level 4, and the tale stops being a fable

variations.cue: In a forest there was a lion.
variations.changed: the place is fronted, which is the commoner order in a written telling and changes nothing else

sentences.usage: The standard opening of a tale, and it is worth learning as one block: one, an animal, a place in the 'in' shape, āsīt. Everything after it moves to the participial past.

mistake.why: The forest is where he WAS, so it takes the 'in' shape vane. vanam is the forest named or entered, and with āsīt it says the lion was a forest.

sentences.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ āsīt iti ucyate.
sentences.cue: It is said that there was a lion in a forest.
sentences.literal: in-forest one lion was quote is-said

words.note: L3-M5's quotative, closing the whole opening sentence so that the passive behind it can be about it.
L4-M7's passive of uktavān's root. Nobody is named as saying it, which is exactly what makes this the written register rather than the spoken one.

sentences.trap: This is the SAME sentence as the one before it, told in a different register. Nothing in it is new vocabulary, and nothing in it is a different event — only the passive and the fronted place do the work.

variations.display: ekaḥ siṃhaḥ vane āsīt iti ucyate.
variations.cue: It is said that there was a lion in a forest.
variations.changed: the place goes back where the spoken telling puts it, which loosens the line without changing the register
variations.script: एकः सिंहः वने आसीत् इति उच्यते।

variations.display: vane ekaḥ śaśakaḥ āsīt iti ucyate.
variations.cue: It is said that there was a hare in a forest.
variations.changed: the actor forks, and the classical frame holds unchanged around it
variations.script: वने एकः शशकः आसीत् इति उच्यते।

variations.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ āsīt iti kathā.
variations.cue: The story is that there was a lion in a forest.
variations.changed: the verb gives way to the noun, which is heavier still and is how a written tale names itself
variations.script: वने एकः सिंहः आसीत् इति कथा।

sentences.usage: The classical opening. Put it beside the sentence before it and the difference is the whole module: same event, same words, and a register apart. Use it when you are quoting a tale rather than telling one.
sentences.script: वने एकः सिंहः आसीत् इति उच्यते।

sentences.display: saḥ siṃhaḥ kruddhaḥ āsīt, ataḥ vane ekaḥ śaśakaḥ bhītaḥ āsīt.
sentences.cue: That lion was angry, so a hare in the forest was afraid.
sentences.literal: that lion angry was, so in-forest one hare afraid was

words.note: L1-M5's 'that one', masculine, pointing back at the lion just introduced. In a tale it is what English does with 'the'.
L3-M6's 'angry', an adjective agreeing with the lion. In this course a feeling is an adjective, so it bends like one.
A hare, masculine, and the tale's other actor. Both ś sounds are the palatal sibilant, the sh of 'ship', and not the retroflex one.
L3-M6's 'afraid', an ordinary adjective and not a participle. bhītā is the shape when the one afraid is female.

sentences.trap: One hare, not all the hares. The plural participial past is written nowhere on this course, so a tale is told about one actor at a time — and this is the sentence where an English speaker would put the whole forest in fear.

variations.cue: That lion was angry.
variations.changed: the consequence drops, leaving only the state the tale turns on

variations.display: saḥ siṃhaḥ śāntaḥ āsīt, ataḥ śaśakaḥ bhītaḥ na āsīt.
variations.cue: That lion was calm, so the hare was not afraid.
variations.changed: both halves flip together, which is the tale that has no story in it
variations.script: सः सिंहः शान्तः आसीत्, अतः शशकः भीतः न आसीत्।

variations.cue: Was that lion angry?
variations.changed: asked rather than told, which is a listener's interruption and not a narrator's line

sentences.usage: The setup. A fable needs exactly two facts before anything happens — who is dangerous and who is afraid — and ataḥ is what ties them together without a word of explanation.
sentences.script: सः सिंहः क्रुद्धः आसीत्, अतः वने एकः शशकः भीतः आसीत्।

sentences.cue: Suddenly the hare spoke to the lion.

words.note: L4-M10's 'suddenly'. It heads the sentence that turns the story and marks a break in what was going on, not merely speed.
The lion as the one spoken TO. This verb takes that person in the -am shape, which is the same shape a thing acted on takes.
L3-M5's past of saying, agreeing with the hare who spoke and not with the lion he spoke to. uktavatī is the shape when a female character speaks.

sentences.trap: There is no vocative in this line and there is not going to be one. An animal addressing another animal is the place a fable most wants that form, and this course writes it nowhere: the person spoken to takes the -am shape and that is the whole of it.
sentences.sound: a-kas-MAAT SHA-sha-kah SIM-ham UK-ta-vaan. akasmāt ends in a dental t that is fully said and not swallowed; at speed akasmāt śaśakaḥ joins with the t shading toward the ś in front of it.

variations.cue: The hare spoke to the lion.
variations.changed: the turn word drops, and the event stops being a surprise

variations.cue: Suddenly a hare spoke to the lion.
variations.changed: the hare is introduced rather than referred back to, which is how a second actor enters late

variations.cue: Suddenly the hare did not speak to the lion.
variations.changed: negated, which in a tale is a real event: the silence is the thing that happens

sentences.usage: The hinge of the tale. akasmāt is the word that tells a listener the setup is over, and a fable that has none reads as a description rather than a story.
sentences.mnemonic: akasmāt is where the story starts.

sentences.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ asti iti śaśakaḥ uktavān.
sentences.cue: 'There is a lion in the forest,' said the hare.
sentences.literal: in-forest one lion is quote hare said

words.note: L1-M3's present tense, inside a quote in a past-tense tale. Nothing shifts for being reported, which is where English would move it back.
L3-M5's quotative, standing AFTER the quoted words. There is no opening mark: iti alone shows where the quote ends.
The hare, now the one speaking. The verb behind him agrees with him, as it always agrees with whoever spoke.
'Said'. It comes after the quote and after the speaker, which is the fixed order for a reported line in this course.

sentences.trap: asti inside a tale told with āsīt is correct. The quote is preserved exactly as it was said, so its tense belongs to the moment of speaking and not to the moment of telling.

variations.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ asti iti śaśakaḥ vadati.
variations.cue: 'There is a lion in the forest,' says the hare.
variations.changed: the narration moves to the present, which is the lively telling a speaker slips into mid-story
variations.script: वने एकः सिंहः अस्ति इति शशकः वदति।

variations.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ asti iti sā uktavatī.
variations.cue: 'There is a lion in the forest,' she said.
variations.changed: a female character speaks, and the past shape forks with her
variations.script: वने एकः सिंहः अस्ति इति सा उक्तवती।

variations.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ na asti iti śaśakaḥ uktavān.
variations.cue: 'There is no lion in the forest,' said the hare.
variations.changed: the quote is negated, which is the same tale with the trick taken out of it
variations.script: वने एकः सिंहः न अस्ति इति शशकः उक्तवान्।

sentences.usage: Dialogue in a tale, and it is the same machinery as reporting what a colleague said: quote, iti, speaker, verb. Nothing about a fable makes it special.
sentences.script: वने एकः सिंहः अस्ति इति शशकः उक्तवान्।

mistake.display: vane ekaḥ siṃhaḥ āsīt iti śaśakaḥ uktavān.
mistake.why: Every word is correct and the quote has been shifted back into the past, which is what English does and this language does not. The hare said asti; iti preserves it, and moving it to āsīt makes him report rather than speak.

sentences.cue: Hearing this, the lion was angry.

words.note: L1-M1's neuter 'this', standing for the whole line just spoken. L3-M2's tat would be a correlative and there is no relative clause here to answer.
L4-M4's absolutive of śṛṇoti. It carries no person and no tense and waits for the finite verb at the end of the sentence.
'Was'. The absolutive in front of it has no tense of its own, so this one word dates both halves of the sentence.

sentences.trap: The absolutive has no subject of its own. Whoever the finite verb belongs to is the one who heard — so idam śrutvā siṃhaḥ means the LION heard it, and nothing in śrutvā says so.

variations.cue: Hearing this, the lion was afraid.
variations.changed: the reaction changes and the frame does not, which is where a retelling actually differs

variations.cue: Hearing this, the lion went into the forest.
variations.changed: a state gives way to an event, and the participial past replaces āsīt

variations.cue: Hearing this, she was angry.
variations.changed: a female character reacts, and the adjective forks with her while the absolutive does not move

sentences.usage: The absolutive is what makes a retelling sound told rather than listed. Two events in one breath, with the first one hanging on the second — an English speaker will write two sentences here and it will sound like a report.

sentences.display: anantaram siṃhaḥ vanam gatavān, kintu tatra siṃhaḥ na āsīt.
sentences.cue: After that the lion went into the forest, but there was no lion there.
sentences.literal: after-that lion forest went, but there lion not was

words.note: L2-M10's longest sequencer, carrying the middle of an account. Like the other three it takes no ending.
The forest as the place gone TO. A neuter noun keeps one shape whether it is named or entered, so no word for 'into' is written.
L1-M2's participial past of gacchati, agreeing with the lion. gatavatī is the shape when the one who went is female.
L1-M7's 'there'. It points at the place just named instead of naming it again, and it takes no ending.

sentences.trap: vanam here and vane three sentences ago are one word. The -e shape is 'in the forest' and the -am shape is the forest itself, whether named or entered — and the verb, not the noun, is what tells you which is meant.
sentences.sound: a-NAN-ta-ram SIM-hah VA-nam GA-ta-vaan, KIN-tu TAT-ra SIM-hah NA AA-seet. gatavān ends in a long ā and a full n; at speed the na āsīt at the end runs together into one long vowel and this course still writes it apart.

variations.cue: After that the lion went into the forest.
variations.changed: the second half drops, and the tale loses the emptiness it turns on

variations.display: tataḥ siṃhaḥ vanam gatavān, kintu tatra siṃhaḥ na āsīt.
variations.cue: Then the lion went into the forest, but there was no lion there.
variations.changed: a shorter sequencer, which moves the tale faster and reads as more spoken
variations.script: ततः सिंहः वनम् गतवान्, किन्तु तत्र सिंहः न आसीत्।

variations.display: anantaram sā vanam gatavatī, kintu tatra siṃhaḥ na āsīt.
variations.cue: After that she went into the forest, but there was no lion there.
variations.changed: a female character makes the journey, and the past shape forks with her
variations.script: अनन्तरम् सा वनम् गतवती, किन्तु तत्र सिंहः न आसीत्।

sentences.usage: The sequencers are what hold a retelling together: prathamam, tataḥ, anantaram, ante. Use them where English would use nothing at all, because this language marks the joints on the surface.
sentences.script: अनन्तरम् सिंहः वनम् गतवान्, किन्तु तत्र सिंहः न आसीत्।

mistake.display: anantaram siṃhaḥ vane gatavān, kintu tatra siṃhaḥ na āsīt.
mistake.why: Motion TO a place takes the -am shape and not the 'in' shape. vane gatavān says he went about inside a forest he was already in, which is not what the tale needs.

sentences.display: ante siṃhaḥ khinnaḥ āsīt, śaśakaḥ santuṣṭaḥ āsīt.
sentences.cue: In the end the lion was miserable and the hare was content.
sentences.literal: in-the-end lion sad was, hare content was

words.note: L2-M10's closer. It tells a listener the tale is finishing, and nothing else in an account does that job.
L1-M9's 'sad', agreeing with the lion. khinnā is the shape when the one who is sad is female.
L1-M9's 'content', agreeing with the hare. The two adjectives at the end are what the whole tale was built to set side by side.

sentences.trap: The two halves share nothing but their shape, and there is no word for 'and' between them. A pair of clauses set side by side is a contrast in this language, and ca would flatten it into a list.

variations.cue: In the end the lion was miserable.
variations.changed: the second half drops, and the tale ends on a loss rather than on a contrast

variations.display: ante siṃhaḥ santuṣṭaḥ āsīt, śaśakaḥ khinnaḥ āsīt.
variations.cue: In the end the lion was content and the hare was miserable.
variations.changed: the two adjectives swap, which is the same tale told by somebody on the lion's side
variations.script: अन्ते सिंहः सन्तुष्टः आसीत्, शशकः खिन्नः आसीत्।

variations.display: ante siṃhaḥ khinnaḥ āsīt iti ucyate.
variations.cue: It is said that in the end the lion was miserable.
variations.changed: the classical register again, with the passive putting the telling at a distance
variations.script: अन्ते सिंहः खिन्नः आसीत् इति उच्यते।

sentences.usage: How a fable closes: the two actors, the two states, side by side, and no comment. The moral comes afterwards as a separate sentence, and a tale that explains itself inside its last line has told the listener they were not following.
sentences.script: अन्ते सिंहः खिन्नः आसीत्, शशकः सन्तुष्टः आसीत्।

sentences.display: ataḥ kruddhaḥ janaḥ ante khinnaḥ iti aham jānāmi.
sentences.cue: So I know that an angry person ends up miserable.
sentences.literal: so angry person in-the-end sad quote I know

words.note: L1-M9's 'so', at the front of the consequence. A moral is a consequence drawn from a story, which is exactly this word's job.
L3-M9's person, singular here. A moral is stated about one person and not about people, because the plural past is written nowhere on this course.
L3-M5's quotative, closing the moral so that the verb behind it can be about it rather than state it.
L2-M8's 'I know', first person, which is the only shape this course writes. A moral is claimed by the teller and by nobody else.

sentences.trap: The moral has no verb inside it. kruddhaḥ janaḥ ante khinnaḥ is two adjectives and a noun and is a complete sentence — adding asti to it would be correct and would also make it heavier than a moral should be.
sentences.sound: A-tah KRUD-dhah JA-nah AN-tay KHIN-nah I-ti a-HAM JAA-naa-mi. The kh of khinnaḥ is an aspirated k and the kr of kruddhaḥ is a plain one: the two openings are the whole difference between the words.

mistake.display: ataḥ kruddhaḥ siṃhaḥ ante khinnaḥ iti aham jānāmi.
mistake.why: The moral is about the lion again, so nothing has been drawn from the tale — it has only been repeated. A moral generalises: the animal in it becomes a person, or it was not a moral.

variations.display: kruddhaḥ janaḥ ante khinnaḥ iti aham jānāmi.
variations.cue: I know that an angry person ends up miserable.
variations.changed: the consequence word drops, and the moral stops being drawn from anything
variations.script: क्रुद्धः जनः अन्ते खिन्नः इति अहम् जानामि।

variations.display: ataḥ kruddhaḥ janaḥ ante khinnaḥ iti ucyate.
variations.cue: So it is said that an angry person ends up miserable.
variations.changed: the classical register: the moral is what is said rather than what the teller knows
variations.script: अतः क्रुद्धः जनः अन्ते खिन्नः इति उच्यते।

variations.display: ataḥ śāntaḥ janaḥ ante santuṣṭaḥ iti aham jānāmi.
variations.cue: So I know that a calm person ends up content.
variations.changed: the same moral from the other end, which is the version a tale about the hare would reach
variations.script: अतः शान्तः जनः अन्ते सन्तुष्टः इति अहम् जानामि।

sentences.usage: The moral, and the one place a retelling may be about something. Keep it to one sentence, generalise off the animals, and claim it with jānāmi rather than asserting it flat.
sentences.mnemonic: Draw it, do not repeat it.
sentences.script: अतः क्रुद्धः जनः अन्ते खिन्नः इति अहम् जानामि।

comprehensionPool.cue: There was once an old man in a village.

comprehensionPool.display: siṃhaḥ vane āsīt, śaśakaḥ api tatra āsīt.
comprehensionPool.cue: The lion was in the forest, and the hare was there too.
comprehensionPool.script: सिंहः वने आसीत्, शशकः अपि तत्र आसीत्।

comprehensionPool.cue: My father told me a story.
There was a path in the forest.

comprehensionPool.display: śaśakaḥ bhītaḥ āsīt, kintu saḥ śāntaḥ āsīt.
comprehensionPool.cue: The hare was afraid, but he was calm.
comprehensionPool.script: शशकः भीतः आसीत्, किन्तु सः शान्तः आसीत्।

comprehensionPool.cue: In the end the lion went into the forest.

comprehensionPool.display: mahyam kathā rocate, yataḥ kathā sukham dadāti.
comprehensionPool.cue: I like a story, because a story gives pleasure.
comprehensionPool.script: मह्यम् कथा रोचते, यतः कथा सुखम् ददाति।

comprehensionPool.cue: It is said that the lion went into the forest.
The story is that the hare spoke to the lion.
There are no people in the forest.
Having heard the story, the boy was content.
